::: {.notes}
My topic is how to implement new customizations in a Quarto website. A lot of Quarto sites start with the same default feeling: clean, but not very personal.

I want to show that customization does not have to mean redesigning the whole site. I will focus on three practical changes: setting a theme system, creating reusable content components, and improving visual scanning. Together, these can make a class website feel more like a real portfolio.
:::

```{=html}
<line x1="568" y1="628" x2="626" y2="628" stroke="#18202b" stroke-width="4" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/>

</svg>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The first customization is controlling the whole site from two files. The first file is `_quarto.yml`, where Quarto stores website-wide settings like the theme, navbar, search, and footer. The second file is `custom.scss`, where I define the visual identity.

The main idea is to name the design choices. In the YAML file, I can tell the navbar to use the theme's primary color with `background: primary`. In the SCSS file, I define what `$primary` actually is. So I would not literally write `$primary` in `_quarto.yml`; the YAML references `primary`, and the SCSS controls the value behind it.
:::


::: {.notes}
The second customization is turning repeated content into components. For example, if my website has several analytics projects, I do not want each project to have a different layout. I want one reusable project card.

In Quarto, I can add a custom class directly in the `.qmd` file, like `project-card`. Then I style that class once in CSS. The sentence in the source, "Built a model to flag high-risk customers," becomes the description in the rendered card. This makes the site look more intentional and also makes new pages faster to build.
:::


::: {.notes}
The third customization is visual hierarchy. A default Quarto page can become a long block of text very quickly. A customized page should tell the reader where to look first, second, and third.

I would use a strong title, colored labels, small metric boxes, and consistent spacing. These are small CSS changes, but they change the reading experience. The goal is not decoration. The goal is faster understanding.
:::

::: {.notes}
My final workflow is simple. First, choose three or four design tokens. Second, connect `custom.scss` in `_quarto.yml`. Third, style one reusable section. Fourth, run `quarto preview` and check the site on desktop and mobile. Finally, run `quarto render` when the site is ready.

My takeaway is that Quarto gives the structure, but CSS gives the personality. With only a few intentional customizations, a class website can start to feel like a real portfolio. I also included my GitHub repo link so students can see the website code in action.
:::
